title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks
authors: Rohan Menon, Chih-Hong Cheng
abstract: Attack success rate (ASR) evaluates jailbreaks against large language models without accounting for repeated calls to the victim model. Yet each additional call gives the deployed system another opportunity to detect the attack and intervene. We introduce $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{STEP}}$, which penalizes additional victim-model calls while retaining binary success judgments. title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting
authors: Arjun Ashok, Mihir Parmar, Palash Goyal et al.
abstract: Recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) can consume covariates in-context, extending zero-shot forecasting to problems driven by external factors. This enables scenario analysis: forecasting how a target responds to events that set covariates to chosen future values. Whether they can do this reliably is an open question. title: A Fisher-Geometric View of Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
authors: Liu Kaiyuan, Zhuang Ziyuan, Ma Haoxuan et al.
abstract: Consolidating specialized foundation models into a unified generalist is a central goal of post-training. Two approaches are in common use: model merging, which is fast but treated as a heuristic, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation, which matches distributions but demands heavy rollout compute and suffers from cross-task gradient conflict. title: Toward Structured Financial Foundation Models
authors: Natraj Raman, Saumitra Mishra, Vamsi Potluru et al.
abstract: Foundation models promise reusable capabilities and step-change performance gains across tasks. In finance, large-scale pretraining of domain-specialized foundation models can advance both goals. However, prevailing architectures and objectives do not by themselves address the combined demands of financial systems: partial observability, interacting entities, asynchronous events, changing regimes, action-dependent outcomes, and rare states with disproportionate consequences. title: RouterWorld: Scaling Conversational AI with Latency-Aware LLM Routing
authors: Jinyang Li, Denis Emelin, Simone Tedeschi et al.
abstract: Conversational AI systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) require routing mechanisms that balance answer quality and response latency at scale. However, existing LLM routing benchmarks assume full observability of all candidate model outcomes, under-emphasize latency as a first-class metric, and fragment evaluation across heterogeneous protocols misaligned with real-world settings. title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Shenli Zheng, Zhou Fang, Yuan Du et al.
abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. title: AfriGuard: Safety and Robust Refusal For African Languages
authors: Israel Abebe Azime, Jesujoba O. Alabi, Iffat Maab et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) designed to interact with users are typically trained to respond appropriately to harmful or toxic content. However, ensuring appropriate responses becomes more challenging in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts, where safety risks may be expressed or interpreted differently. title: VeriCUA: Learning Proactive Verification for Reliable GUI Agent Rewards
authors: Zhizhou Wang, Yaxi Lu, Zhong Zhang et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning for computer-use agents increasingly relies on proactive reward agents that interact with the post-execution GUI environment to verify what recorded screenshots cannot reveal. The reliability of such verification hinges on two coupled decisions: what to check and when to stop. Existing methods leave these decisions to prompted foundation models. title: GAIDA: Generative AI for Human-in-the-Loop Document Annotation
authors: Islam Mesabah, Ali Elhosary, Priyabanta Sandulu et al.
abstract: Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. title: PhyPro-FM: A Physics and Prompt-Guided Graph Foundation Model for Contingency Analysis
authors: Xu Yang, Zhanyuan Sheng, Chenhui Lin et al.
abstract: The continuous evolution of next-generation power systems, characterized by the high penetration of renewable energy resources and dynamic topology variations, poses formidable challenges to traditional N-1/N-2 contingency analysis in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
authors: Nikita Dragunov, Matvey Mikhalchuk, Anton Razzhigaev
abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Capability-Focused Evaluation with Structural Diversity for Time Series Foundation Models
authors: Hongyin Zhang, Mingyi Xiang, Rongzhao Chen et al.
abstract: Static public benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically have fixed and narrow test distributions. Their repeated reuse encourages benchmark-specific tuning, making reported performance reflect adaptation to the fixed test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. In addition, a single aggregate score cannot fully characterize model capabilities across distinct temporal structures and input relationships. title: Towards More Granular Reasoning: Mapping the DSA Transparency Database Taxonomy to Platform Terms and Conditions Using Large Language Models
authors: Alyson Ranucci, Eline Leijten, David Graus
abstract: Article 24(5) of the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires providers of online platforms to submit every content moderation decision they make, with a corresponding Statement of Reasons (SoR), to the DSA Transparency Database (DSA-TDB). Such decisions are classified against seventeen high-level attribute categories that categorize the primary reason for the moderation decision. title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
authors: Yizhou Yang, Jiahong Fu, Zhiwu Wang et al.
abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. title: Budgeted Attack Scheduling for LLM Red-Teaming: The Roles of Static Priors, Semantic Guidance, and Online Feedback
authors: Zhicheng Fang, Han Sun, Jiachen Lei et al.
abstract: As jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) become increasingly diverse, red-teaming has come to rely on large libraries of jailbreak prompts and attack strategies to evaluate the robustness of victim models and their defense settings. title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
authors: Changshuo Liu, Jiaqi Zhu, Wenqiao Zhang et al.
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
authors: Debojeet Ghosh, Shreyansh Kumar, Ayushman Garg
abstract: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo
abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. title: EvalRx: Agentic Diagnosis and Verified Repair of Foundation Models
authors: Jiaqi Liu, Ruinan Jin, Yitong Tang et al.
abstract: Model evaluation reveals where models fail, but rarely why or whether a proposed fix genuinely works. We introduce EvalRx, an open-source agentic framework for statistically grounded model diagnosis and repair. EvalRx discovers systematic failure modes, explores candidate mechanisms, formulates falsifiable hypotheses, and verifies them by executing frozen, pre-specified tests before using supported diagnoses to guide tiered repair. title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models
authors: Seungjong Sun, Hyunmin Jun, Minsik Yoon et al.
abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
authors: Haoqun Cao, Yurun Yuan, Tengyang Xie
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. title: Inside the Scorer: Mechanistic Evidence on Rubric Control in LLM-Based Automated Essay Scoring from 25 Base Models
authors: Chungche Huang, Po-Ya Angela Wang, Shu-Kai Hsieh
abstract: Automated essay scoring (AES) using large language models (LLMs) offers promising use cases for language assessment, yet high-stakes testing requires scores that are both controllable and verifiable, which current LLM-based scorers lack. Given that, we investigate whether LLM-based scorers form distinct internal representations for individual scoring rubrics and whether these representations can be independently controlled. title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
authors: Qihan Huang, Lingxia Zhang, Guye Zhang et al.
abstract: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. title: From Black Box to Controller: Inference-Time Steering of LLM via Feature Amplification
authors: Keqi Chen, Zekai Sun, Yuhua Wen et al.
abstract: Inference-time steering is crucial for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications, where they must flexibly adjust behavior preferences. For instance, a model should dynamically adjust its caution level based on the risk of the scenario. This requirement introduces a challenge: modulating the intensity of LLM preferences. title: CVaR-RMD: CVaR Selection Pressure for Robust Metaheuristic Discovery
authors: Ruodai Cui, Li Niu
abstract: Large language models have recently been used to discover heuristics through iterative program search, offering a promising approach to automated algorithm design. However, candidates selected by average performance may degrade across instance families, random seeds, and problem scales because mean-based objectives can obscure rare but severe failures. title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
authors: Desheng Xu, Hanglin Li, Tianchen Song et al.
abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
authors: Zhengao Li, Chuxu Zhang, Yushun Dong
abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
authors: Anamaria-Roberta Hartl, Levente Zólyomi, Michael List et al.
abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
authors: Lu Sun, Xiangyi Zhang, Xiangyang Zhu et al.
abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. title: Breaking Diffusion: Parallel Reasoning with Draft Refinement
authors: Jaesang Yu, Seoyeon Byun, Yun Wang et al.
abstract: Drafting an answer allows a reasoning model to reconsider each decision in the context of the others. Yet repeated diffusion denoising does not ensure that individually plausible token updates form a better answer together. We introduce Draft Refinement Language Models (DRLMs), which use a single denoiser to propose parallel revisions and evaluate a candidate draft. title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Preference Reward Models with Evolving Penalties
authors: Afonso Baldo, António Farinhas, Marcos Treviso et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models has moved from preference reward models to verifiable rewards, which sustain much longer optimization. Preference models are prone to reward hacking: the policy raises their score without improving response quality, or even while degrading it. Yet for open-ended tasks, where quality can neither be verified nor fully written down as rubrics, they remain valuable. title: When Coding Agents Outpace Review: Evaluating PRD-Driven Development in Mature Enterprise Repositories
authors: Tianqi Liu, Yandong Guan, Songze Li et al.
abstract: Coding agents increasingly undertake development tasks in mature enterprise repositories, yet existing benchmarks offer limited insight into whether they fulfill complete Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) and where delivery breaks down. Issue resolution and development from scratch leave incremental PRD fulfillment underexplored, while isolated tests provide incomplete evidence of business and integration requirements. authors: Ruotian Peng, Yuanyi Ren, Shuaiqi Liu et al.
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
authors: Jiuzhou Han, Abhishek Bijay Mishra, Trevor Cohn et al.
abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
authors: Yuxuan Wu, Miaopei Lin, Qiufang Ying et al.
abstract: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
authors: Abhinav Khattar, Aishwarya Chhabra, Ameya Velingker et al.
abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. title: LOOP: Recovery-Aligned Iterative Layer Pruning via On-Policy Distillation
authors: Liang Xu, Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou et al.
abstract: Layer-level pruning is attractive for large language model (LLM) deployment as it reduces the model size while preserving a dense architecture that can be efficiently executed on standard hardware. Current methods typically follow a one-shot paradigm, which first removes selected layers to reach a target model size and then performs additional training to recover model capabilities. title: Neither Over- nor Under-Constrained: Evaluating LLM Personalization under a Constraint Qualification Audit
authors: Xuran Li, Guanqin Zhang, Imran Razzak et al.
abstract: Accurate evaluation of LLM personalization is hindered by current evaluation paradigms that over- or under-constrain the response space, yielding frequent false rejections and false acceptances. title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yuanze Xu, Tianzhu Ye, Hui Sun et al.
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. title: Selecting and Composing Agent Design Patterns: Industrial Case Evidence and Controlled Reference-System Experiments
authors: Jia Huang, Bingsheng Ru, Bo Liang et al.
abstract: Agent pattern catalogs describe architectural alternatives, but engineers also need evidence for selecting and composing them. We extend a cognitive-function--execution-topology framework with an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. The study combines two industrial case accounts, a contributor's collaboration design, seven practitioner workshops, and executable fault-injection experiments. title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
authors: Ruhan Wang, Kishan Panaganti, Dongruo Zhou
abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
authors: Lilin Xu, Linyang He, Kaiyuan Hou et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. authors: Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaohan Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. authors: Soukaina Alaoui Ismaili, Jean-Sebastien Dessureault
abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. authors: Hyunji Alex Nam, Michael Dennis, Natasha Jaques et al.
abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. authors: Junwei Yao, Yongxi Zhou, Zike Yang et al.
abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. title: RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents
authors: Xinying Cai, Bin Hu, Mingyu Jin et al.
abstract: Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
authors: Zhiwei Liu, Zhujun Lan, Jielin Qiu et al.
abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
authors: Tao Jiang, Benjamin Navet, Yousouf Taghzouti et al.
abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
authors: Yanan Ma, Yang Wang, David Le et al.
abstract: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Zhen Tan et al.
abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Ziwen Kan et al.
abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner et al.
abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
authors: Ziyang Liu, Jiakang Yuan, Jiayuan Fan et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
authors: Ran Zhou, Zehui Kong, Fanyu Lin et al.
abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
authors: Shreyas Kulkarni, Uttam Gurram, Madhav Kanda et al.
abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. authors: Jiabin Fan, Matthias Lindemann, Zita Marinho et al.
abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. title: Understanding the Benefits of Scaffolds through Computational Separations
authors: Jingchu Gai, Adam Block, Andrej Risteski
abstract: Inference-time harnesses, i.e., external procedures that call a model many times and keep state across calls, can substantially improve model capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the benefits of using such harnesses and the extent to which these benefits can be internalized through training. More precisely, we conceptualize a harness $\mathcal{A}$ as an arbitrary wrapper around a base model $M$ and attempt to distill a student model from the harness's traces. title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
authors: Yuqiao Wen, Lili Mou
abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. title: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering
authors: Emanuele Mezzi, Gertjan Burghouts, Fabio Massacci et al.
abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final

title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
authors: Joong Ho,  Choi, Sherine George et al.
abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. title: Fluent but Fallible: Benchmarking Hallucination and Factual Reliability in Large Language Models
authors: Osama Shabih, Dayam Nadeem, Shahab Saquib Sohail et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced natural language processing and artificial intelligence applications through their capabilities in reasoning, text generation and knowledge retrieval. However, LLMs are still vulnerable to two important challenges: hallucination, generating factually incorrect or fabricated content, and response deviation, meaning systematic deviations from ground-truth responses. title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
authors: Rohit Saxena, Alessandro Suglia, Marek Rei et al.
abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks

title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
authors: Joong Ho,  Choi, Aditya Paul et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 2

title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Yiming Bian, Yun-Shiuan Chuang et al.
abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
authors: Kyle Stein, Andrew Arash Mahyari, Guillermo Francia et al.
abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. title: Evaluating Tibetan Speech Recognition Across Dialects and Adaptation Regimes: A Multi-Granularity Analysis
authors: Jacob Moore, Sheng Li
abstract: Tibetan speech recognition is usually evaluated with character or syllable error rates because the writing system does not mark word boundaries. These metrics can rank systems differently and respond differently to adaptation failures. We combine character error rate, syllable error rate, and segmented word error rate in one evaluation framework. title: Fundamental Impossibility Results in AI Safety: Trading Off between Desiderata
authors: Ida Mattsson, Ratip Emin Berker, Emanuel Tewolde et al.
abstract: Is there a fundamental tradeoff between desiderata for safe AI systems, such as harmlessness and helpfulness? We answer by formalizing the interaction between AI systems and users as a game with three players: a defender and an attacker that are computationally or informationally bounded, and an AI that provides public advice and is less constrained. title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
authors: Wenyue Chen, Yuhan Cheng, Ruixin Yang et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
authors: Jalil Alva, David Harper, Abigail E. Thornton et al.
abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. title: African Languages AI Safety Readiness Report
authors: Israel Abebe Azime, Jesujoba O. Alabi, Tajuddeen Gwadabe et al.
abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) across languages and domains, AI safety has emerged as a critical global concern. However, due to resource constraints, research and development efforts tend to prioritize a limited number of high-resource languages, leaving many others, especially those spoken in Africa, underrepresented. While existing research on language "resource-ness" has largely examined whether sufficient resources are available to develop language technologies

title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
authors: Chenhan Lyu, Amir Rahmani
abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label.

title: The Culture Within: Towards Mechanistic Understanding of Cultural Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Samee Arif, Furkan Danisman, Angana Borah et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate across culturally diverse settings, yet existing evaluations largely measure cultural behavior at the output level. We introduce CultureLens, a reference-grounded benchmark and mechanistic study of how LLMs use cultural information. CultureLens contains 9,261 scenarios across 75 countries and systematically varies country, value, true-norm, and contradictory-norm evidence. title: Exposing Vulnerability Monoculture Through Systemic Adversarial Robustness
authors: Leo Elmecker-Plakolm, Lukasz Szpruch, Avishek Joey Bose et al.
abstract: Beneath the apparent diversity of foundation models lies an increasingly homogeneous technical stack of common training pipelines, distillation methods, and data. These shared algorithmic choices can expose an otherwise distinct model ecosystem to concentrated risks leading to a vulnerability monoculture. title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
authors: Avi Gupta, Nilotpal Sinha, Vishnu Raj et al.
abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we pro

title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
authors: Beichen Lu, Honglin Bao, Qi Huang et al.
abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. title: When Models Know but Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
authors: Rui Melo, Andre Catarino, Claudia Mamede et al.
abstract: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
authors: Jiho Lee, Bingquan Zhang, Lin Ting Liang et al.
abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds

title: Diagnostic Analysis for Large Language Model Reasoning
authors: Xinyu Liu, Dongqi Fu, Jun Wu
abstract: Reasoning structures (e.g., chains and graphs) are increasingly used for probabilistic inference, factuality verification, and uncertainty estimation, but their structural reliability is rarely evaluated directly. We test whether this reliability holds through a proposed two-stage diagnostic evaluation in open-ended multi-hop QA. Stage 1 tests different capabilities required to construct reasoning graphs, showing that graph reliability varies with topology, prompt design, and model family. Stage

title: Profile-DP: Differential Privacy for User-Controlled Profile Release in Personalized LLM Inference
authors: Mingchen Li, Zifan Peng, Kewei Sha et al.
abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on profile-conditioned inference, pairing public requests with rich, user-specific facts. This paradigm exposes the user profile itself, together with the user's explicit sharing preferences. We introduce Profile-DP, a policy-aware local differential privacy framework designed specifically for user-profile release in personalized LLM inference. title: Preference-Aware Pareto Steering for Multi-Task Speech LLMs
authors: Liuyuan Jiang, Vishal Sunder, Samuel Thomas et al.
abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) perform multiple tasks, including automatic speech recognition (ASR), timestamp prediction (TS), and speech translation (ST). Joint training of speech LLMs creates task trade-offs, yet standard training with fixed loss weights does not generally control the resulting trade-off according to deployment preferences. title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
authors: Lada Kudláčková
abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). title: ClockMark: Adaptive and Host-Dependent Watermarking for Large Language Models
authors: Yupeng Qiu, Han Fang, Ee-Chien Chang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) watermarking operates on the next-token distribution that evolves during generation. In streaming generation, each sampled token becomes part of the text and affects subsequent distributions. Embedding therefore proceeds with a changing host, unlike classical watermarking, which adapts embedding to an existing host signal. title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
authors: Tong Ding, Caiwei Tian, Dongmin Bang et al.
abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
authors: Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen, Tianfan Xue et al.
abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. title: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
authors: Hengyu Ye, Songhua Hu
abstract: A repair action proposed by a large language model (LLM) specifies which records to change and how to change their values. A failed action may still contain a useful choice of records or a useful update, depending on how the two are paired. We introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates selected records (targets) from the applied change (an update). title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
authors: Akash Gokul, Srijan Bansal, Yingbo Zhou et al.
abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. title: Guided Diffusion for Trustworthy Synthetic Text Generation
authors: Qi Pang, Hanshen Xiao, Andre Manoel et al.
abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
authors: Phurinat Polasa, Thanapon Thanadunpremdet, Phatthanasak Kraiduang et al.
abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Lihong He, Lucian Popa, Marina Danilevsky
abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
authors: Jianing Yin, Ziyi Chen, Hao Wang et al.
abstract: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. title: VHDLBench: Benchmarking and Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for VHDL-Based Chip Design
authors: Patrik Drazic, Benaoumeur Senouci, Boualem Benatallah
abstract: The rapid evolution of digital circuit complexity demands innovative approaches to hardware design automation. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have influenced software development, their application to Hardware Description Language (HDL) generation remains largely unexplored, particularly for VHDL. This paper presents a comprehensive study for AI-assisted digital circuit design, addressing gaps in current Electronic Design Automation workflows. The work introduces a VHDL dataset of 18,500+ sy

title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou, Gaoxiang Yuan
abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
authors: Silvia Fernández-Sabido, Jorge Reyes-Magaña, Jesús Adrián Chay Tun et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous

title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
authors: Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park et al.
abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. title: The World as Viewed by 136 Countries: An Open, Curated, Annotated, and Multilingual Dataset of 118 Million State Media Articles
authors: Bryan Li, Samar Haider, Grace Kim et al.
abstract: State media outlets often project their governments' narratives to target both domestic and foreign audiences. Because this content is plentiful and free to access, it appears widely in the web corpora that large language models (LLMs) are trained on and that retrieval systems draw from. However, the prevalence of state media in these corpora and its potential influence on LLM outputs remain largely unexplored. title: Design and Cross-Domain Evaluation of an Agent Execution Harness
authors: Saurav Joshi, Manas Gupta, Ashwin Venkatesh Raman et al.
abstract: Completing complex tasks with language-model agents requires coordinating planning, execution, and review so the final result addresses the user's original objective. We present an agent execution harness that keeps the original objective separate from a revisable plan and an execution record. A planner assigns scoped tasks, workers produce outputs and artifacts, and a reviewer examines results against the original request before submitting or requesting additional work. title: Learning Which Device to Call: Online Tool Grounding for LLM Agents in IoT
authors: Yichen Liu, Xiaochong Jiang, Haoran Yu et al.
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. title: Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
authors: Jinu Lee, Shraddha Barke
abstract: Symbolic constraints (programmatic, deterministic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic verification of LLM agents' tool calls, but existing approaches primarily enforce predefined safety policies rather than tool dependencies in complex tool environments. We explore whether symbolic constraints can be mined from environments and observations beyond predefined policies, and whether they can improve end-to-end task performance. title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
authors: Yunlong Deng, Yan Li, Xing Hu et al.
abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context.
